absent: Full mapping engine sequences beyond the advance helper and small-read fast path, including opener and closer implementations and error recovery.
Writeback and read finish helpers, folio batch handling, bio allocation and submission details, and integrity processing.
Direct transfer executor internals, bounce handling, alignment enforcement and overwrite-only validation beyond flag meanings.
Active kernfs hierarchy implementation including locking order, reference counting, lookup, mutation and notification delivery.
Namespace lifecycle, extended-attribute storage, permission checks, mount and superblock setup beyond context layout.
Validity cookie format and comparison logic for cached mapping revalidation and long-write refresh timing.

findings.text: Write path customization groups folio provisioning with mapping revalidation and optional synchronous loading. One callback obtains a folio for a given iteration position and byte count. A second callback releases that folio with owning inode, file position, copied amount and folio reference. A predicate lets the filesystem confirm that a cached extent mapping still reflects internal extent state, using private data such as a sequence marker saved when the mapping was created. An optional loader fills a folio span for an iteration. The predicate executes while the framework keeps the folio for that position locked; when no custom loader exists the framework falls back to issuing a block layer read.

Low iteration selectors each occupy a distinct bit position from zero through seven. Position zero asks for block allocation on write. Position one marks zeroing where unmapped gaps may be bypassed. Position two asks for range state disclosure used by extent query helpers. Position three marks fault-time mapping. Position four selects direct transfer. Position five forbids blocking. Position six limits work to pure overwrites. Position seven marks range unsharing. Each selector is a single bit.

Higher iteration selectors cover direct-access mapping, write atomicity and caching hints. Direct-access selector has two build forms: one sets bit eight when the feature is active, the other yields numeric zero when inactive. Bit nine asks for torn-write protection. Bit ten carries a hint to avoid caching. Direct-access value must be treated as configuration dependent.

Mapping lifecycle uses three callbacks collected in a compact table. The opening callback creates mappings for an inode over a position span with flag word and two mapping slots. The closing callback finalizes a span with start, span length, advancement distance, flags and mapping reference. The stepping callback advances an iteration using current and alternate mappings plus remaining length. The table holds one pointer per phase in open, close, step order.

Iteration cursor records owning inode, current file offset, remaining byte count, start offset of the active mapping, numeric progress status, flag word, primary mapping descriptor, secondary mapping descriptor for copy or share cases, optional folio batch reference and opaque private reference. Primary descriptor tracks the extent under processing; secondary supports operations needing a source extent.

Advance helper follows two paths based on whether the active mapping still has length. When length remains, it optionally calls a completion callback with inode, mapping start, trimmed span, advancement amount, flags and mapping, then asks a continue helper whether more work remains and stops early unless continuation requests another round. When no length remains or continuation requests more, it calls the opening callback with inode, position, length, flags and both mapping slots, treating negative outcomes as failures and non-negative as a request to proceed. Two generator macros emit thin wrappers binding either opening alone or opening with completion to this advance signature.

Boundary helper aligns post-write offsets to the filesystem block size derived from the inode. A zero written count aligns the start offset downward to its block start. A positive count aligns the sum of start plus written bytes upward to its block end.
Deallocation callback type describes hole removal over an inode span. It receives owning inode with start offset and length and produces no result.

Completion record links into a chain and tracks small flag storage, target inode, extent byte size, deferred completion counter, saved error code, parent link for grouped completion, file offset, device start sector, filesystem private reference, integrity context reference and an embedded block transfer descriptor. The embedded descriptor must stay at the trailing end so the enclosing record can be located from the descriptor address. A helper converts a descriptor address back to its enclosing record using container address calculation.

Completion markers use bit zero for shared coverage, bit one for unwritten coverage, bit two for boundary condition and bit three for direct origin. A combined non-merge mask joins shared, unwritten and direct bits while leaving boundary out. Flag storage in the completion record is sixteen bits wide.

Writeback contract pairs a range processor with a submitter and a context bundle. The range processor handles a folio slice identified by position, length and end offset, may span large regions but must run at least once per folio to coordinate with mapping invalidation, may reuse a prior mapping while still valid, and obliges a finish notification for every accepted span regardless of later success, reporting processed byte count or negative error. The submitter finalizes a context accumulated by prior range calls, reporting success or negative error, with a nonzero error input requesting error completion. The context bundle holds current mapping, inode, writeback control reference, operation table reference, folio tally and pending private state.

Buffered read state bundles operation table reference, active folio, optional readahead control, opaque read state with its file offset and integrity context. The operation table provides a required span loader that must be followed by a finish notification whether loading succeeds or fails and reports success or negative error, an optional dispatch hook for queued reads and an optional allocation pool pointer allowing filesystems to source new block descriptors from their own pool.

Direct transfer operation table offers a completion callback receiving control block, transfer size, error code and flag word and returning status, plus a dispatch callback receiving iteration, block descriptor and file offset. An optional pool pointer permits filesystem-specific descriptor allocation. Filesystems needing private descriptor data must override dispatch to attach that data and replace the termination callback with a wrapper that performs local post-processing and then delegates to the shared direct termination helper.

Direct extent markers use bit zero for unwritten coverage and bit one for copy-on-write coverage. Direct control selectors use bit zero to force waiting, bit one to restrict to overwrite, bit two to mark partial handling, bit three to assert block alignment and bit four to request bounce buffering. Each marker is a single distinct bit.

Small direct read fast path builds an iteration from the control block file, position and iterator length with direct mode set. It takes no action on empty length and declines mappings larger than one block, extending past file size, targeting encrypted inodes or failing a preceding write drain. It forwards nonblocking intent from control flags, brackets mapping with begin and end accounting, obtains a mapping through the caller supplied opener and on success hands off to a shared simple-read executor. Declined cases return without mapping.

Swap activation through this mapping path is unavailable in the routed build and reports a generic input-output failure. Two inline read conveniences build a read state bound to the shared block read operations, one with a single folio and one with a readahead control, then delegate to generic folio read and readahead engines with no additional private context.

Sharding width has two build forms: one derives bit count from processor count capped at thirty two through a doubled binary logarithm, the other fixes bit count at one. Total shard count equals one shifted by that bit width.
Hierarchy-wide mutation protection uses a sharded array of node mutexes whose length equals total shard count. Each shard guards a subset of nodes selected by hash.

Node kind occupies the low four bits with directory value one, file value two and link value four. One mask retains those low four bits for kind; a second mask retains the complement for flags. State bits use decimal sixteen for activated, thirty two for namespace, sixty four for sequence display, one hundred twenty eight for mmap, two hundred fifty six for dependency tracking, five hundred twelve for hidden, one thousand twenty four for suicidal, two thousand forty eight for suicided, four thousand ninety six for empty directory, eight thousand one hundred ninety two for release support and sixteen thousand three hundred eighty four for removing.

Hierarchy creation options use value one to start nodes deactivated and invisible until explicit activation for atomic appearance, value two to enforce extra open permission checks requiring read or write bits and implemented handlers even with override privilege, value four to advertise handle-based export support, value eight to allow user extended attributes and value sixteen to forbid renames across parents.

Directory payload counts subdirectories, anchors a balanced tree of children extending through the node tree link, stores owning hierarchy reference in this payload to save space and keeps a monotonic revision for detecting changes during negative lookup validation. Link payload holds a reference to the target node. Attribute payload holds operation table reference, RCU-guarded open-node reference, size value and a chain link for notification traversal.

Core node record joins reference and active counters with optional dependency state, RCU-guarded parent and name references that require helper access when moves are possible, tree linkage, namespace tag, combined name hash, flag half-word and mode, a discriminated payload for directory, link or attribute use, a sixty four bit identifier serving as inode number on wide builds and split into number plus generation on narrow builds, opaque private reference, attribute store reference and deferred cleanup linkage.

Hierarchy-level table exposes option display, directory creation from parent with name and mode, directory removal, rename with node plus new parent and new name, and path display with hierarchy context. Each operation reports status as an integer.

Open instance joins published node, file, sequence iterator and private references with internal locking, event tracking, list linkage, preallocated buffer storage, atomic write bound, mapped and released markers and memory operation hooks. The operation table offers optional open and release around sequence setup, sequence display and traversal callbacks with sequence private pointing at the open instance, raw span read and write bounced through kernel buffers with page-granular partials or atomic bound enforcement, an optional preallocation mode incompatible with sequence display, plus poll, map and seek hooks. Raw reads larger than a page complete partially; writes obey the atomic bound when set.

Mount setup record stores hierarchy root, optional namespace tag and filesystem magic number, plus a flag recording whether the mount helper allocated a new superblock. The first three describe the request; the flag reports allocation outcome.

Per-open synchronization uses a primary mutex and a separate buffer-setup mutex. Parent, name and open-node references require RCU-safe handling; directory child trees and revision counters assume the holder excludes concurrent writers.

Completion pairing is strict: accepted writeback spans always need a finish notice even when later stages fail; accepted read spans always need a finish notice after data arrival even on failure; custom direct dispatch must chain to the shared termination helper after local work. The block descriptor must remain last in its completion record for address recovery. Merging is forbidden across differing shared, unwritten or direct origins.

Direct use of parent and name fields is unsafe when renames or moves can occur; dedicated accessors must be used. Namespace activation is valid only on empty directories and otherwise warns. Writes exceeding a configured atomic bound fail as too large while unbounded writes fragment at page size. Preallocation cannot be combined with sequence display. Inert fallback builds return not-implemented, null, false, zero or error pointers instead of performing hierarchy work.
Active namespace enablement checks that the target is a directory and that its child tree is empty, issuing one-time warnings on violation, then sets the namespace state bit.

Inert fallback definitions standardize unavailable hierarchy services. Creation of directories, files and links plus name lookup, rename, attribute change, poll, extended-attribute access and tree acquisition report not-implemented or error-pointer results. Parent lookup, namespace walk, conversions from dentry or superblock, namespace retrieval and inode acquisition return null. Reference acquire and release, activation, removal, notification, context release, superblock teardown and global initialization perform no action. Self-removal reports false and root-flag query reports zero. Non-namespaced walk delegates to namespaced walk with no tag; simple directory creation delegates to namespaced creation with root ownership and no tag; one namespace-enable form does nothing and two name-path printers do nothing.
Header inclusion guard defines a private marker macro to prevent repeated processing of the kernel filesystem header.
